transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-14 15:30 UTC | Duration: 38m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Leo Patel, Aria Gomez (Redwood)  Sara Gomez, Tom Reynolds, Priya Singh, Evan Lowe (Nova Financial)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from our side, I'm Maya, your AE, with Leo our solution engineer and Aria who will be your CSM if we move forward.
[00:10] Sara Gomez: Hi, Sara here. thanks. high level we're evaluating Redwood to power internal customer support summarization and a few RAG flows, plus some higher throughput batch jobs. Main ask today: how do we pick between Hosted, Dedicated and Private for a two week POC and then production?
[00:25] Leo Patel: Great, thanks Sara. we'll run through typical success criteria, what we need for benchmarks, and what each deployment mode gives you. quick question — do you have an initial target p95 latency or cost constraint?
[00:40] Tom Reynolds: We're hoping short queries (single-turn summarization) to be under 300ms p95, ideally closer to 200 when possible. For RAG flights (multi-step) we expect more tokens and can tolerate higher. Our CFO'll be sensitive to cost per 1M tokens; need to show economics vs current setup on AWS.
[01:05] Priya Singh: Also security — we need audit logs, KMS integration, and SOC2 evidence. if we go private we need to understand network options (VPC peering or on-prem).
[01:20] Maya Chen: Makes sense. typical decision drivers are latency/cost, data control/compliance, and ops complexity. Hosted gives fastest time-to-value and low setup overhead, Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation with reserved capacity, and Private gives max control — VPC and on-prem options with full auditability.
[01:40] Leo Patel: For the POC we usually recommend starting either Hosted with strict SLOs to validate accuracy and latency, or Dedicated if you already have strict throughput/latency SLAs and want repeatable benchmarking. Private is usually chosen if compliance prohibits cloud-hosted secrets or you need air-gapped on-prem.
[02:05] Evan Lowe: Our legal team is open to hosted if data is encrypted at rest and in transit and if we get SOC2 + contractual DPA. But Priya wants KMS & customer-managed keys for production.
[02:20] Maya Chen: That's a common path — hosted for POC, then move to dedicated or private for production depending on the benchmark results and compliance review.
[02:30] Sara Gomez: OK what do you need from us to run a benchmark?
[02:35] Leo Patel: Ideally: a week's traffic sample (anonymized) or a synthetic trace that matches concurrency and token distribution; expected avg tokens per request; peak concurrency and qps; and a small eval set with correctness metrics and thresholds. Also any latency SLOs and the region you'd prefer.
[02:55] Tom Reynolds: We can provide a 7-day trace and a sample set of 200 evaluation prompts. average tokens per summarization is around 450 tokens request + 120 tokens response. Batch jobs are larger — ~3k tokens. Peak concurrency is around 120 concurrent requests during business hours, with burst to 300 for short windows.
[03:20] Leo Patel: Good, that gives us enough to size. for Hosted, you care less about reserved GPUs but cost can vary by model and token. for Dedicated, we size GPU pool to handle sustained concurrency — with continuous batching for cost efficiency and lower tail latency.
[03:40] Maya Chen: One quick note on KV cache and RAG — if you have heavy RAG reuse patterns (same docs, many similar prefixes), prefix/KV caching can dramatically reduce cost and latency. we can instrument that in the benchmark.
[03:55] Sara Gomez: We do have a lot of reuse for policy docs, so caching sounds promising. can you quantify token savings?
[04:05] Leo Patel: Roughly, with 30% prefix reuse you might see 20-40% token cost reduction depending on sequence lengths and cache hit rates. we'll model this in the benchmark plan.
[04:20] Priya Singh: on encryption — for Hosted do you support bring-your-own-key and customer managed KMS?
[04:25] Maya Chen: Hosted supports envelope encryption with Redwood-managed KMS; we also offer customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private — the Private option also supports HSM integrations if needed. sometimes the transcript transcription shows 'Redwood Private' misread as 'Red wood private' in older notes, sorry — ignore that.
[04:45] Tom Reynolds: For Dedicated, what's the typical lead time to provision reserved capacity?
[04:50] Leo Patel: For standard dedicated pools it's usually 2–4 weeks to provision depending on region and hardware. if you need specific SKUs or on-prem, that can be longer. but for POC we can provision a short-term dedicated pool or run benchmarks on Hosted with dedicated-like configuration to mimic production.
[05:10] Evan Lowe: Budget question — do you provide an estimate for cost per 1M tokens for our workloads?
[05:15] Maya Chen: We can provide ballpark numbers once we see your workload distribution; we'll run our cost model and give hosted vs dedicated amortized cost. Dedicated typically lowers unit cost if you have sustained throughput.
[05:30] Sara Gomez: Success criteria — from our side I'd propose: 1) p95 latency < 300ms for single-turn summarization, 2) end-to-end accuracy F1 > 0.82 on evaluation prompts, 3) cost/capacity projection for production at X qps, 4) security acceptance (KMS + audit logs). Is that aligned?
[05:55] Maya Chen: That's a solid set. we usually add operational criteria — e.g., ability to trace per-request token costs, and a fallback policy (automatic downgrade to a smaller model or region) if tail latency spikes.
[06:10] Priya Singh: For audit logs — do you store raw request/response in logs? we need options to mask PII and retention controls.
[06:20] Aria Gomez: You can configure logging to redact PII; we support configurable retention windows and export of audit logs to your SIEM via syslog or cloud logging sink. we'll include those config details in the security doc.
[06:35] Tom Reynolds: How do you handle model rollouts and compatibility? we want to pin model versions and have canary rollouts.
[06:45] Leo Patel: Redwood supports model pinning, canary/A-B, and automatic fallback to compatible variants. the console shows per-route model and token breakdowns so you can compare regressions easily.
[06:58] [small crosstalk] Sara: that's helpful.
[07:05] Leo Patel: For the benchmark plan — we propose two phases: Phase 1: Hosted synthetic benchmark to validate latency/accuracy with your eval set (2–3 days). Phase 2: Dedicated short-term pool or Hosted extended benchmark with realistic trace (3–7 days) to validate cost & tail behavior.
[07:25] Maya Chen: Timeline wise, if you can share traces this week, we can run phase 1 next week and aim to have results and a sizing recommendation by end of next week.
[07:35] Sara Gomez: That timeline works. any blockers on our side?
[07:40] Leo Patel: Just the traces and an agreed eval rubric. also need to confirm models you want tested — open models vs Redwood curated models. which families do you prefer?
[07:50] Evan Lowe: We'll start with an open Llama-style model and a Redwood-verified medium chain-of-thought variant. not sure of exact name.
[07:58] Maya Chen: we'll map the model names — sometimes the auto transcription or internal docs misread model variants. we'll include exact model IDs in the benchmark plan.
[08:10] Tom Reynolds: When you run benchmarks, can you simulate our concurrency pattern? our busiest hour has 120 sustained concurrency and spikes to 300 for 10–15 minutes.
[08:20] Leo Patel: Yes we'll replicate that. we'll also instrument KV cache hit rates and simulate batch jobs separately to size GPU memory for long sequences.
[08:32] Priya Singh: A few security follow-ups — do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001? any pen test reports?
[08:40] Maya Chen: Redwood maintains SOC2 and we have an ISO certification. we'll send the attestation and a redacted pen test summary; full reports require an NDA which we can facilitate.
[08:55] Sara Gomez: Good. on deployment mode decision criteria, can you summarize pros/cons?
[09:00] Leo Patel: Quick summary: Hosted — pro: fastest onboarding, lower ops, immediate scaling; con: less control over keys and infra (though we do support some KMS integration). Dedicated — pro: reserved capacity, predictable latency/cost, isolation; con: commit needed and lead time for provisioning. Private — pro: full control, VPC/on-prem, HSM/KMS flexible; con: highest ops overhead and longer setup time. For many customers the path is Hosted POC -> Dedicated for production if economics justify -> Private only if compliance requires it.
[09:35] Evan Lowe: That matches our thinking. If Dedicated reduces cost by >20% we may go that route.
[09:42] Maya Chen: We'll quantify that in the cost model.
[09:46] [10:00 — 20:00 section summarizes technical deep dive]
[09:50] Leo Patel: Some implementation notes — sequence length distributions matter for kernel selection and memory. if you have many long sequences (3k tokens), we need to use quantization-friendly kernels and possibly model sharding. we'll note this in the sizing doc.
[10:08] Tom Reynolds: For batch jobs can we run them during off-peak windows to reduce contention?
[10:12] Leo Patel: Absolutely — scheduling batch during low traffic hours is common. we also support burst capacity on Dedicated for short windows.
[10:20] Sara Gomez: On measuring accuracy, we'll provide a gold set and expected thresholds. we'd like Redwood to run the eval and provide per-model F1/ROUGE metrics.
[10:30] Maya Chen: we'll include that.
[10:32] Priya Singh: Any SLA differences between Hosted and Dedicated?
[10:36] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and uptime targets as part of reserved contracts. Hosted has published SLOs but enterprise-grade SLAs are available on Dedicated and Private with support tiers.
[10:52] Evan Lowe: Regarding costs — can we get a three-year TCO projection?
[10:56] Maya Chen: We'll produce a 1/3/5 year projection after benchmarks that includes amortized dedicated costs, expected token volume growth, and caching effects.
[11:08] [Silence/notes]
[11:10] Sara Gomez: ok recap and next steps please?
[11:14] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) Nova to provide 7-day sample trace and 200 eval prompts; 2) Redwood to run Phase 1 hosted benchmark and Phase 2 realistic benchmark; 3) Redwood to deliver sizing worksheet, pricing sheet, SOC2 + security docs; 4) Schedule 2-hr benchmark run w/ Leo. timeline: artifacts due by 2026-08-18, Phase 1 next week, sizing + recommendation by 2026-08-24.
[11:40] Priya Singh: we'll aim to get the security questionnaire answers by 2026-08-20.
[11:45] Maya Chen: Great. any final Qs?
[11:48] Tom Reynolds: Not for now. thanks.
[11:50] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and links to docs.
[11:55] [meeting ends]
notes: References to artifacts: Redwood sizing worksheet (link shared in chat), security package (SOC2 attestation PDF link), benchmark plan (google doc link). Customer will anonymize trace before sharing.
